title: Zaghouan-Carthage Roman aqueduct
summary: A Roman aqueduct that carried spring water from Zaghouan to Carthage, about 132 km counting its branches, with 17 km on arcades; its arches reached 38 m in the Miliane valley. Built in the 2nd century CE, it was interrupted in Vandal times and rebuilt in places under the Hafsids in 1250-1267.

uncertainty.note: Carthage Magazine believes it was built between 120 and 131 CE; Hydria says the 2nd century CE; npj Heritage Science says Hadrian's 128 CE visit prompted the order. Start is 120, end of the span is 2nd century. End is the present: sections remain.

phases.description: Built in the 2nd century CE (Hydria); believed built between 120 and 131 (Carthage Magazine).
Supplied Carthage; the pages opened give no dated changes in this span.

Water supply interrupted during the Vandal occupation, 439-533, then repaired; the Byzantine period brought abandonment and stone-robbing (npj Heritage Science). Hydria says it worked until at least 536.
After Carthage fell to the Arabs in 698, the aerial sections were destroyed again, though later restored with different features (npj Heritage Science).
New sections built under Hafsid Sultan Abu Abdullah Mohammed I, 1250-1267, to supply his palace and Tunis (npj Heritage Science).

reviewer_note: Linear (shape wall as the nearest path form). 38 m is the figure npj Heritage Science gives for the Miliane valley; a Roman-aqueduct database snippet I did not open gives 33.65 m and 20 m, and the Carthage and Hydria pages open give no heights. Length 132 km includes branches; the main conduit is just over 90 km. Phase gaps (533-698, 200-439) are not sourced as intact. Pin is OSM's Temple of Waters node at the Zaghouan end.
